1065.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1065.hook: Mahisha changes shape again and again, and the goddess drinks, laughs, and tells him to roar while he can
1065.carry: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1065.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1065.howItsDone: The goddess slaying Mahisha, Mahishasuramardini, is a familiar image of Durga, and during Durga Puja and Navaratri Hindus worship images that show her with her foot on the buffalo and Mahisha emerging from it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, each god gave the goddess something of his own, the mountain gave her a lion, and her breaths became armies.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `EACH GOD GIVES FROM HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: The generals are dead, their armies scattered. Now the buffalo himself comes onto the field. In the third chapter Mahisha arrives in his own form, and the text makes him frightening: he tramples her troops with his hooves, flings them with his horns, lashes them with his tail. His hooves crack the ground; his breath tosses mountains. He charges her lion. And the goddess, the text says, grows angry. It's the scene shown in images of her as Mahishasuramardini, she who crushes the buffalo demon: a goddess, a lion, a buffalo at her feet. Here is how the text tells it.
screen: `THE BUFFALO HIMSELF.` → `HE CHARGES THE LION.` → `THE SCENE THE IMAGES FREEZE.`

segments.voice: She throws her noose around him, and he stops being a buffalo. He's a lion. She cuts off its head, and a man with a sword stands in its place. She shoots him down, and he's a great elephant, dragging her lion with his trunk. She cuts off the trunk, and he's a buffalo again, shaking the worlds. Every time she has him, he becomes something else. Then, in the middle of battle, the goddess stops and drinks from her cup, again and again, laughing, her eyes going red. Mahisha, full of his own strength, bellows and hurls mountains at her with his horns. And she speaks to him. In paraphrase: roar, roar for a moment, you fool, while I drink. When I've killed you, the gods will be roaring here instead. Then she leaps, sets her foot on his neck and pierces him with her spear. Pinned, he starts to come out of the buffalo's mouth in his real form, only halfway out, still fighting, and she cuts off his head with her great sword. The gods rejoice. Look at the shape of it. Mahisha's power is changing form; he never stays one thing long enough to be held. She meets each shape as it comes, and then she stops. She isn't hurried by him. When she moves again, she moves once, and he's pinned and has to show himself.
screen: `A BUFFALO, A LION, A MAN, AN ELEPHANT.` · `SHE STOPS, DRINKS, AND LAUGHS.` · `ROAR FOR A MOMENT, YOU FOOL.` · `HALF OUT OF HIS OWN SKIN.` · then, large: `SHE WAITS UNTIL HE SHOWS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Settle with whatever today still holds undone, and don't solve any of it: let its noise keep going like a roar in the distance. Breathe in slowly, as if taking a long drink, breathe out slowly, and let the next thing wait a few breaths. If you pray, rest in the goddess, or in God, by the names you already use; if not, let the breath be the place you stand.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the end of its second story: Mahisha the shape-shifter, pinned under the goddess's foot until he has to show himself.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. In the middle of the fight she stopped to drink, and wasn't hurried. Until tomorrow.

1066.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1066.hook: the gods praise the goddess after the battle, ask why she didn't simply burn the demon with a glance, and receive a promise
1066.carry: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1066.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1066.howItsDone: The gods' hymn in the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, sometimes called the Shakradi Stuti after Indra (Shakra), is recited as part of the whole text and is also chanted on its own by some devotees of the goddess.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Mahisha changed shape again and again, until the goddess pinned him and he had to show himself.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `ROAR FOR A MOMENT.`

segments.voice: If the goddess could end Mahisha with a single look, why fight at all? The gods themselves ask it. In the fourth chapter the buffalo is dead. The gods, Indra at their head, bow with necks bent and bodies thrilled, and praise her. Partway through their hymn they wonder out loud: you could have burned him to ash just by looking. Why didn't you? A strange question for a victory song, and their own answer is stranger. Today, the hymn, and the promise she leaves before she vanishes.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `WHY NOT ONE LOOK?` → `A HYMN, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: The hymn begins wide. In paraphrase, the gods bow to the goddess who spread out the whole world by her own power, whom even Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma can't fully describe. Then it comes down into ordinary houses. She is good fortune in the homes of those who do good, and misfortune in the homes of those who do harm; understanding in the hearts of the learned, faith in the good, modesty in people of noble birth. In this hymn she isn't only on a battlefield. She's at the kitchen table, in what a house becomes. Then the question, and the gods answer it themselves. In paraphrase: so that the demons, purified by your weapons, might reach the higher worlds. Even toward enemies, your thought is kind. These demons had done enough harm to deserve a long time in hell, and you killed them in battle so they might reach heaven instead. In the gods' own hymn, the sword is a kind of mercy. Then the goddess tells them to choose a boon. They say, in paraphrase: our enemy is dead, so everything is done. But if we remember you again, come and end our worst troubles, and may whoever praises you with this hymn prosper. She agrees, and vanishes. Hold on to that promise: remembered in trouble, she will come. The next chapter opens with new demons, and the gods, cornered again, remembering exactly this.
screen: `FORTUNE IN THE HOMES OF THE GOOD.` · `WHY NOT BURN HIM WITH A LOOK?` · `EVEN TOWARD ENEMIES, KIND.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND I WILL COME.` · then, large: `THE SWORD AS A KIND OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has made life harder for you, not the hardest, just someone, and breathe with whatever rises. Then, without excusing anything they did, let one small wish form for their good, that they find some peace; you don't have to mean it completely. If you pray, hold them before God or the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let the wish ride out on the breath.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the gods' hymn after the battle: fortune in good homes, kindness even toward enemies, and a promise to come when remembered.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Even toward enemies, the hymn says, her thought is kind. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1067.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1067.hook: the third story begins: new demons, a hymn to the goddess who dwells in all beings, and a marriage proposal she answers with a vow

1067.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1067.howItsDone: The refrain of the fifth chapter, beginning 'ya devi sarvabhuteshu', is also chanted on its own by some Hindus, at home and in temples, including during Navaratri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods asked why the goddess didn't burn Mahisha with a look, and she left a promise: remember me in trouble, and I will come.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND I WILL COME.`

segments.voice: To the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness: bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again. That's the shape of a refrain the gods sing in the fifth chapter, changing one word each time. The third story has begun. Two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven, seized the work of the sun, the moon and the wind, and thrown the gods out. So the gods do what they promised. They remember her, go to the Himalaya, and start to sing.
screen: `TWO DEMON BROTHERS TAKE HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS REMEMBER HER.` → `THEY START TO SING.`

segments.voice: Listen to what changes. In paraphrase: the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness. As understanding. Sleep. Hunger. Shadow. Power. Thirst. Patience. Modesty. Peace. Faith. Loveliness. Good fortune. Memory. Compassion. Contentment. Mother. And, near the end, as error. Each time: bow to her, again and again. It isn't only the noble things. Hunger is there, and sleep, and thirst. Even error. In this hymn the goddess isn't up on a mountain away from ordinary life; she's in the states a living being passes through in a day. Then the story moves. Parvati, Shiva's wife, comes down to bathe in the Ganges and asks: who are you praising? From her own body a goddess steps out and answers: this hymn is for me. Two of Shumbha's servants, Chanda and Munda, see her on the mountain and run to their master with news of a woman so beautiful that a king who owns every treasure ought to have her too. So Shumbha sends a messenger with a proposal: marry me, or my brother. The goddess smiles. In paraphrase: what you say is true. But long ago, without much thought, I made a vow. Only the one who defeats me in battle, who takes away my pride, who is my equal in strength, can be my husband. Let him come and win me. The messenger warns her she's being foolish. She doesn't move.
screen: `IN ALL BEINGS AS CONSCIOUSNESS.` · `AS HUNGER, AS SLEEP, AS ERROR.` · `A GODDESS STEPS OUT OF PARVATI.` · `ONLY ONE WHO DEFEATS ME.` · then, large: `BOW TO HER, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Notice what's here, one state at a time, the way the hymn lists them: hunger, tiredness, some patience, some restlessness, a memory, each given a breath. Don't sort them into good and bad; the hymn didn't. If you pray, bow inwardly to the goddess at each one, as the gods do; if not, simply let each be seen.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the third story's opening: a refrain to the goddess who lives in all beings, even as hunger and error, and her vow to Shumbha.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Hunger, sleep, even error: the hymn makes room for them all. See you tomorrow.

1068.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1068.hook: a demon general undone by one syllable, and Kali springing from the goddess's frowning brow
1068.carry: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1068.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1068.howItsDone: Kali and Chamunda are worshiped in Hindu temples, and the seventh chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, where Kali springs from the goddess's brow and is named Chamunda, is recited as part of the whole text.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods bowed to the goddess in all beings, and she answered Shumbha with a vow.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `IN ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: One syllable: hum. That's all it takes in the sixth chapter. Furious at her vow, Shumbha sends a general named Dhumralochana with an army and an order: drag her here by the hair. The general shouts at her to come quietly. She answers, in paraphrase: you're strong, and you've brought an army. If you take me by force, what can I do? He rushes at her. She makes one sound, hum, and he's burned to ash. Her lion takes care of the army. And the goddess is about to show a face the story hasn't shown yet.
screen: `DRAG HER HERE BY THE HAIR.` → `ONE SOUND: HUM.` → `A FACE NOT SEEN YET.`

segments.voice: In the seventh chapter Shumbha sends Chanda and Munda, the servants who first told him of her, with a bigger army. They find her seated on her lion on a golden peak, smiling, and come at her with bows and swords. Her face goes dark with anger, dark as ink. And from her frowning forehead another goddess springs out. The text describes her plainly. Kali. Dark, gaping mouth, lolling tongue. Thin, wrapped in a tiger skin, a garland of human heads, a skull-topped staff and a sword in her hands. Her roar fills the sky. She tears into the army, swallowing elephants whole with their riders and bells, crunching chariots in her teeth. She seizes Chanda by the hair and cuts off his head, then Munda's, and carries both back to the goddess, laughing, as a gift. The goddess names her: because you've brought me Chanda and Munda, you'll be known as Chamunda. So Kali comes not from outside but from the goddess's own brow, at the moment the threat comes close. The same goddess who smiled on the mountain carries this fierce face inside her. And that closes the first week of year four. A king and a merchant who couldn't let go. Vishnu's sleep. Every god's gift, and a lion. A shape-shifter pinned. Kindness to enemies. The goddess in all beings. And now Kali. One goddess, seen from more and more sides.
screen: `HER FACE GOES DARK AS INK.` · `KALI SPRINGS FROM HER BROW.` · `CHANDA AND MUNDA: CHAMUNDA.` · `THE WEEK: ONE GODDESS, MANY SIDES.` · then, large: `THE FIERCE FACE WAS INSIDE HER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you'd stand up for, picture it threatened for just a moment, and notice what rises, a straighter back, a firm jaw, without acting on it: strength, not cruelty. Then let calm come back alongside it, breath by breath, the way the goddess was smiling and fierce at once. If you pray, bow to the goddess or to God in your own words; if not, let the breath hold both.

1069.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1069.hook: the powers of the gods come out as goddesses, and Raktabija, whose every drop of blood becomes another demon
1069.carry: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1069.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1069.howItsDone: The goddesses who come out of the gods in the eighth chapter are known together as the Matrikas, the Mothers, and groups of them are carved and worshiped in some Hindu temples.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Last week ended in the Devi Mahatmya with one syllable, hum, and Kali springing from the goddess's own brow, named Chamunda. A new week begins.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `KALI, NAMED CHAMUNDA.`

segments.voice: Every drop. That's the problem in the eighth chapter. His generals dead, Shumbha sends out his whole army, and something new happens. From the bodies of the gods, their powers step out, each a goddess in that god's own form. From Brahma, one on a swan, with prayer beads and a water pot. From Shiva, one on a bull, holding a trident. From Vishnu, one on Garuda, the great bird. From Indra, one on an elephant, with a thunderbolt. A boar-faced goddess. A lion-faced goddess. They gather around the goddess. Then a demon walks out to meet them: Raktabija. Blood-Seed.
screen: `SHUMBHA SENDS HIS WHOLE ARMY.` → `THE GODS' POWERS STEP OUT.` → `A DEMON NAMED BLOOD-SEED.`

segments.voice: First the goddess does something surprising. From her own body comes one more power, fierce, howling like a pack of jackals, and she gives Shiva himself a job: go to Shumbha and Nishumbha as my messenger. Give heaven back and go home to the underworld, or come and fight. Because Shiva was her messenger, she's called Shivaduti. The demons choose to fight. Then Raktabija. His power is in his name: whenever a drop of his blood falls to the ground, a new demon rises from it, just as strong. The goddesses strike him with thunderbolt, spear, discus, trident, and each wound makes it worse. Soon the field is full of him, and the gods are terrified. So the goddess, smiling, turns to Kali. In paraphrase: open your mouth wide, and take in every drop before it touches the ground. Kali does. As the goddess strikes, Kali drinks the blood and swallows the new demons as they rise. The drops stop landing. Drained, Raktabija falls. Notice what wins. Not a bigger weapon; every weapon only made more of him. What wins is catching the thing before it can grow again. Some readers hear in Raktabija the way a resentment or a craving multiplies each time it's fed. The text leaves that open. What it shows is Kali's open mouth, and a field that finally empties.
screen: `SHIVA SENT AS HER MESSENGER.` · `EVERY DROP BECOMES A DEMON.` · `EACH WOUND MAKES IT WORSE.` · `KALI CATCHES EVERY DROP.` · then, large: `DON'T LET THE DROPS LAND.`

segments.voice: Let a small irritation come to mind and watch one thought grow from it, then another: that's the multiplying. Gently go back to the first one, without feeding or fighting it, and let it settle on the breath out before it can land; if it multiplies again, come back again. If you pray, ask for help in your own words; if you don't, let the breath be what catches it.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its eighth chapter: the gods' powers as goddesses, Shiva sent as a messenger, and Raktabija, beaten when Kali caught every drop.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Every weapon made more of him; an open mouth caught the drops. A new week, well begun.

1070.howItsDone: The goddess's words to Shumbha in the tenth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya are recited as part of the whole text, and some Shakta teachers cite them when explaining that the many goddesses are forms of one goddess.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Raktabija multiplied with every drop of blood, until Kali caught each one.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `CATCH EVERY DROP.`

segments.voice: It's an old insult: you didn't really do it; somebody did it for you. In the ninth chapter the younger brother, Nishumbha, falls. Even then, another figure rises out of his chest shouting stop, and the goddess laughs and cuts off its head. Now only Shumbha is left, his brother dead, his army gone. In the tenth chapter he looks across at the goddess, surrounded by Kali and the other goddesses, and throws the insult. In paraphrase: don't be so proud, Durga. You fight leaning on the strength of others.
screen: `NISHUMBHA FALLS.` → `ONLY SHUMBHA IS LEFT.` → `YOU FIGHT WITH OTHERS' STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: The goddess answers, in paraphrase: I am alone here in the world. Who else is there besides me? Look, you fool: these are my own powers, going back into me. And they do. Brahmani on her swan, the goddess of Shiva's trident, the goddess on Garuda, the boar-faced one, the lion-faced one: the text says they all enter her body. The field is suddenly empty but for two: Shumbha, and Ambika, alone. All along she has seemed to have helpers: Kali from her brow, goddesses from the gods' bodies, troops from her breath. Shumbha took them for outside help. Her answer is that there never was anyone else; in her words, every one was her own power, in another form. Then the last fight. They battle with every weapon, then bare hands. Shumbha seizes her and leaps into the sky, and they fight in the air with nothing to stand on. At last she whirls him around and throws him down, and as he rushes at her one last time she pierces his chest with her spear. He falls, and the text describes the whole world going calm. The rivers run in their courses again, the winds blow gently, the sun shines clear. Hindu teachers read her line more than one way. Some hear a teaching about the one goddess behind every form of the divine. Others hear the story simply saying who she is. The text just shows it: the goddesses walk back into her, and she stands alone.
screen: `I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.` · `THE GODDESSES GO BACK INTO HER.` · `THE MANY WERE ALWAYS ONE.` · `A FIGHT IN THE SKY, THEN STILLNESS.` · then, large: `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that ended recently, a long task, a hard conversation, a worry that came to nothing, and instead of replaying it, notice the quiet that came after. Let the breath run in its own course, the way the rivers did, and let the shoulders, the jaw and the hands loosen. If you pray, rest in God or the goddess in your own words; if not, let the stillness be enough.

1071.howItsDone: Some Hindus who recite the whole Devi Mahatmya finish with the thirteenth chapter's boons to the king and the merchant, and the eleventh chapter's hymn to Narayani is also chanted on its own.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Shumbha said the goddess fought with borrowed strength, and she answered: I am alone here in the world.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Remember the forest? A king who'd lost his kingdom, a merchant thrown out by his own family, both asking a sage why knowing doesn't help. Year four began with them. Every story since, the sleeping Vishnu, the buffalo, Kali, Raktabija, Shumbha, has been the sage's answer to the king's question: who is this goddess? Now the battles are done. One more hymn, one more promise, and then the book walks back into the forest, to the two men who were listening the whole time.
screen: `BACK TO THE FOREST.` → `EVERY STORY WAS AN ANSWER.` → `WHAT WILL THEY DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: In the eleventh chapter, after Shumbha falls, the gods praise her once more, calling her Narayani, and ask her to be gracious to the whole world. Her promise is bigger than before. In paraphrase: whenever trouble rises from the demons, I will come down and destroy the enemy. She even names future appearances. In one, during a terrible drought, she will feed the world with plants grown from her own body, and be called Shakambhari, she who bears the greens. In the twelfth chapter she tells the gods what hearing this story brings to those who recite and listen. Then the thirteenth, the last. Medhas finishes: this is the goddess I told you of. She draws you into confusion, and she can set you free. Go to her. So the king and the merchant go to a riverbank, make an image of the goddess out of earth, and worship her there a long time, with offerings and their whole attention. She appears and asks each what he wants. The king asks for his kingdom back in this life, and a kingdom that won't be lost in the next. She grants it. The merchant, who couldn't stop worrying about the family that threw him out, asks for something else. In paraphrase: the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine. She grants that too. Two men, the same stories, two requests, and the text doesn't rank them. The book that began with two worries ends with two answers.
screen: `THE GODDESS AS NARAYANI.` · `WHENEVER TROUBLE RISES, I WILL COME.` · `AN EARTH IMAGE BY A RIVER.` · `A KINGDOM, AND FREEDOM FROM I AND MINE.` · then, large: `TWO WORRIES, TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Let the goddess's question sit quietly in you: what do you want? Let the first, practical answer come, the kingdom, and notice it kindly; then wait a little longer for a quieter one underneath, the merchant's kind, without choosing between them. If you pray, bring both before the goddess or God in your own words; if not, let the question rest on the breath.
The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess, read whole: a book that begins with two men in a forest who can't let go, and ends with each of them asking her for what he wants.
